items.content_excerpt: I gave coding agents a private leaderboard, the way Kaggle does. The overfitting I expected didn't show up. Guessing did. A coding agent writes the code, writes the tests, runs the tests and then tells you they pass. In the context of competition, the agent is the contestant, the organiser and the scoreboard all at once. Machine learning ran into this a long time ago and settled on a fix. On Kaggle you tune against a public leaderboard you can see, and you are ranked on a private one you can't. Nobody gets to report their own accuracy, because a score you can see is a score you can tune to. I was curious and experimented that on coding agents. In practice that is a handful of separate model sessions. One writes public tests from a spec. Another writes hidden tests from the same spec. A third writes a reference implementation, and any hidden test that doesn't pass on it gets thrown away. Then the implementing agent works in a sandbox where it can't read the hidden suite, and the hidden suite decides whether the work is accepted. None of it is new. It is a holdout set. It is Goodhart's law. It is the QA team writing the acceptance tests so that developers don't mark their own homework. Two things made me want to revisit it anyway. The first is that "all tests pass" has become the main thing we accept from an agent, and it comes from the party that wrote the tests. We wouldn't take that from a contractor, and we don't take it in an ML paper. The second is price. Separation of duties used to cost a second team. An independent test writer now costs a few dollars and under half an hour. There was also a question I couldn't answer in advance, and it turned out to be the one that mattered. Kaggle's hosts hold the true labels. Who holds them for a ticket? My hypothesis was the Kaggle one. Agents would learn the visible tests and fail the hidden ones. That didn't happen. The first 90 runs produced one overfit. It was a real bug, a regex with two capture groups and code that reads the second and the fourth, and the public tests just happened to be too short to trip it. So I wrote harder specs: concurrency, compliance rules, a wire protocol I invented. Across the 230 runs I later re-graded, there were three real overfits. Nobody cheated, either. In about 2,500 sandboxed runs, no agent edited a test or touched the harness. So I had a clean negative result. items.title: The model inside the server: Network design for inference on a few GPU nodes
items.story_key: story|title:the model inside the server network design for inference on a few gpu nodes
items.content_excerpt: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become increasingly pervasive in the data centre. While many documented architectures cover large-scale inference and training, there is something to be said for what happens when you need only a few Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) nodes. This smaller scale can be the right fit when each request is served by one replica, the user count is internal, and the priority is latency or privacy rather than training throughput. A few examples of when a few nodes are enough (there are others beyond these three): Now, this is where designing for some of these models gets tricky. The network problem is not how the GPUs talk to each other. It is how requests, long-lived streams, and occasional bulk transfers behave on the network that’s already in place. Consider a basic setup of 4 servers × 8 GPUs, running a Llama 3.3 70B model with vLLM for an internal application like those described above. The model file is about 141 GB, too large for a single 48 GB or 80 GB GPU, so each server spreads that file across the GPUs in its own chassis. One server holds the whole model and can answer a request without help from the others. GPUs in the same server talk over NVLink or Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe), and none of that traffic needs to leave the chassis. What crosses a Network Interface Card (NIC) is ordinary traffic. Requests come in, and token streams go out. Weights and container images move when a node is built, a process starts cold, or a model version changes. Metrics, logs, and the Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) talk to systems that are already present in the infrastructure. What happens when a model is too large for one GPU? This one’s easy — it gets split across the GPUs in the same server. vLLM, a widely used open-source inference server, documents two ways to do that: But this is all local to the server. What actually leaves your NIC is the front-end flow, where the application sends a prompt and the server responds over Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS). For a chatbot, think about the answers being streamed back to the client. That stream is tiny. At about 300 bytes per message and 50 messages a second, one stream is 120 kbit/s, and a thousand of them is 120 Mbit/s. Bandwidth at this stage is not the problem; session count is. items.content_excerpt: Apargon runs .papp files: personal apps your AI writes, double-click & it works. Create desktop apps with any AI, for macOS, Windows, and Linux. Each app opens in its own window, with its own icon, menus, and menu bar or tray icon. It can ask for notifications, global shortcuts, and always-on-top windows. No account, no cloud. Each app is one .papp file on your disk: plain HTML, with <meta> tags that ask for any extra permissions. No installer, no server, no build step. Double-click it to run it. Send it to share it. Apargon is a reverse browser. A browser gets all of the internet and none of your computer. Apargon flips it: an app reads your local disks, writes only its own folder, and reaches no site unless you say yes. It runs in a sandboxed window. Any coding agent can write one from a prompt: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or a local model. Because every app is an HTML file on your disk, it's malleable software too: open it, change anything you want, save, and the window reloads. Installers for macOS ( .dmg ), Ubuntu 24.04 ( .deb ), and Windows ( .exe ) are on the latest release . Double-click a .papp file to open it, or run open notes.papp (macOS) or apargon notes.papp (Linux). Apargon offers to install the agent skill ( skills/papp/SKILL.md ) on first run. To install it manually: Without permission tags, a .papp file opens immediately. It can read your local disks, write to its own folder, open file pickers, store OS-sealed secrets, set a custom icon, native menus, and tray icon, print, and live-reload on save, with no network. <meta> tags in <head> unlock more, one capability at a time. One folder or one CLI tool doesn't give the app your other files or the internet. Any tag that lets data leave your computer, changes files outside the app's folder, watches you, or works with its window closed asks in a plain-English popup first. items.title: CoT-Proxy: Cross-Format Transfer for Distilling Long-Horizon Policies
items.summary: Reasoning models become long-horizon agents through reinforcement learning or, more cheaply, through fine-tuning on a stronger teacher's trajectories, which contain the teacher's chain-of-thought as well as its actions. The standard fine-tuning approach imitates both, yet the strongest teachers are closed models whose chain-of-thought is hidden behind an API. We show that the chain-of-thought can be left out altogether and that the long-horizon policy can be distilled from the teacher's actions alone. The student is trained on these trajectories with its reasoning block left empty, while a KL loss on a replay buffer of its own generations limits drift from its initial model. Surprisingly, the policy learned from these trajectories with an empty reasoning block carries over to inference with thinking enabled, where the student reasons in its own style while acting like the teacher, an effect we call cross-format transfer. Distilling the actions of Qwen3.6-27B raises the task success of Qwen3-4B on AppWorld from 7% to 18% and that of Qwen3-32B from 12% to 25%. We further introduce CoT-proxies, short summaries of the teacher's reasoning placed after the empty reasoning block, which raise Qwen3-4B further, to 35%. Since neither actions nor CoT-proxies need the hidden chain-of-thought, the recipe applies unchanged to closed teachers. Distilling GPT-5.6 Luna from its visible outputs and the reasoning summaries its API returns raises Qwen3-4B from 7% to 48% on AppWorld and from 3% to 28% on SWE-bench Verified.

items.title: iWAM: Efficient Action Prediction from World Models without Explicit Future Prediction
items.summary: World-action models (WAMs) build policies on pretrained video-generation models, on the premise that predicting how a scene evolves helps determine how to act. However, generating future scenes is expensive for real-time control. This motivates efficient proxies for future imagination, but how to train such proxies without sacrificing action-prediction quality remains unclear. An effective proxy need not generate a high-resolution frame; it only needs to provide enough information to distinguish between possible futures. This leads to the design principle behind iWAM: rather than denoising an entire future frame, can we condition the action policy on intermediate features from a single video-model evaluation? We show that the answer is yes. Exploiting the reversible dynamics of flow-matching models, we invert each training future into the corresponding latent noise vector. However, a single velocity evaluation at this latent does not necessarily yield informative features for action prediction. We therefore learn a bidirectional flow map that amortizes future-generation computation, enabling a single model evaluation to provide effective conditioning features. At inference, we sample a latent noise vector from the prior and condition the policy using just one video-backbone forward pass. Across simulated benchmarks and real robots, iWAM recovers the generalization benefits of WAMs while substantially reducing its inference cost.

items.title: Worth the Wait? How Response Time and Streaming Shape Judgments of Generative AI Answers and Chatbot Engagement
items.summary: Answers from generative AI chatbots built on large language models (LLMs) now arrive at very different speeds: reasoning models deliberate before replying, while response caches can return a stored answer at once. Blind preference votes, which rank these models, are read as judgments of their text, and if delivery matters, faster answers are expected to gain. Research on the labor illusion and on how text appears on screen suggests instead that an answer which unfolds as it is written is credited over the same answer shown at once. We test these accounts with three sources of variation in natural use. First, compar:IA, a French government chatbot arena, answered repeated prompts, by a random draw, either with a fresh answer streamed as it was written or with a stored earlier answer from the same model, shown at once. Within the same prompt, a replay lowered an answer's chance of winning a decisive blind vote by 25.8 percentage points. The same stored text won 57% of its decisive votes when streamed and 29% when replayed, and voters called it less complete, more superficial and more often incorrect when replayed. Second, provider congestion slowed streamed answers. In 324,029 conversations, slower answers earned no detectable net credit in the vote, but a slower first exchange made visitors less likely to ask a follow-up question. Third, in 4,378,514 WildChat replies from everyday ChatGPT use, replies slowed by congestion made users less likely to continue. Delivery moved blind votes, in the direction opposite to the one the arena's designers expected, while waiting cost follow-up questions that a comparison between two answers cannot register when both are slow. The results bear on how AI services cache and stream answers, how they budget latency, and how preference leaderboards evaluate models.

items.content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
items.summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
items.content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

items.title: Draft Calibration for Speculative Decoding: Accelerating LLM Serving by Matching Draft and Target Distributions
items.summary: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model (LLM) inference by employing a lightweight draft model to propose draft tokens and allowing the target model to verify the new tokens in parallel to improve inference-time compute utilization. The speedup relies on the acceptance probability of draft tokens in target verification, which is directly related to the gap $\|p-q\|_1$ between the target distribution $p$ and the draft distribution $q$. In this paper, we study draft calibration of speculative decoding to improve the speedup of speculative decoding, where we employ post-hoc methods to calibrate the draft distribution to mitigate the distribution gap. We observe that though current community open-source draft models may learn the top candidate token correctly, they are generally underconfident compared to the target model, suggesting a consistent distribution mismatch. To mitigate the effect of this mismatch on the acceptance rate of the draft models, we try various post-hoc calibration methods, including standard temperature scaling and token-wise calibration. Our results suggest that a standard temperature scaling applied to the draft distribution improves the acceptance length by up to approximately 10\% with almost no additional cost across different tasks. Throughput analysis further verifies that this improvement in serving efficiency. Analysis of more general calibration methods reveals further potential room for improvement.

items.title: RoboRecast: Intent-Preserving Demonstration Augmentation via Diagnosis-Driven Optimization
items.summary: Collecting diverse real-world manipulation demonstrations is costly, motivating the use of simulation to augment existing demonstrations for robot policy learning. When objects, layouts, or robots change, transferring motions from a source demonstration can produce behavior that is semantically implausible or physically infeasible in the new setting. We introduce RoboRecast, an agentic optimization framework that preserves the interactions required by the source task while jointly optimizing the simulated scene and robot motion to make those interactions executable in the target setting. When an interaction fails, the agent uses simulation feedback to diagnose the cause, revise the relevant scene or motion parameters, and test whether the revision resolves the failure. This flexibility allows RoboRecast to generate synthetic data from both human and robot demonstrations and to adapt them to new layouts, objects, and robot embodiments. When target demonstrations are available, adding RoboRecast data improves policy success on both real-world single-arm and simulated bimanual tasks. Even without demonstrations in the target configuration, RoboRecast adapts source demonstrations to support policy learning with new objects or robot embodiments.

items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966c2d0>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966e6d0>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966d010>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966dd10>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966df10>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966ead0>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7fbec966e3d0>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.330
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added sign-in to organizations managed in Anthropic's Enterprise Admin Console: after claude auth login, Claude Code applies the organization's settings and uses its cloud provider or gateway
  • Added easel, a built-in mod that draws charts when asked and under MCP metrics results, on Pro, Max and, where available, Team and Enterprise on macOS and Linux; turn automatic charts off in /config
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_FULL_SIGN_IN_LINK=1 to print the full sign-in link, if the short one shows an error or a script reads values from it
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --start-dir / SELF_HOSTED_RUNNER_START_DIR to have Claude start its work in a folder of a repository, while settings and hooks load as without it
  • Added a notice in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions when a plugin marketplace can't be fetched because its repository isn't one of the session's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a notice when Anthropic-managed git refuses a plugin's own repository, naming the plugin and what to do
  • Added commandPrinted to claude plugin install --json results, true when the plugin's install command wrote to stderr, and commandFailed when it exited with an error, was killed or timed out
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_registered_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order issued to registration accepted, on orchestrator-spawned runners
  • Added claude_code_self_hosted_runner_order_to_first_session_seconds to the self-hosted runner's /metrics: seconds from work order to first session handed over, on runners started for a session
  • Fixed Claude Code freezing for up to several minutes right after compacting a very long conversation
  • Fixed WebFetch freezing the session for minutes on some pages, and returning an empty result for some others
  • Fixed ExitWorktree and the worktree exit dialog deleting a worktree that another running Claude Code session was working in
  • Fixed changes to user settings being lost when several Claude Code processes saved them at the same time
  • Fixed --continue and --resume opening an empty session or failing when the last saved message had a missing or invalid timestamp
  • Fixed the first prompt after a sleep of two minutes or more waiting three minutes on a connection that had died, on Linux and WSL
  • Fixed turns failing with "JSON schema is invalid", and session files growing by many megabytes, when many MCP tools have an input schema that the API refuses
  • Linux: Fixed Bash commands waiting seconds and showing no file diff for the rest of a session in slow repositories with large ignored folders such as node_modules
  • Windows: Fixed Bash commands running slower for the rest of a session after Git Bash took 10 to 60 seconds to start, on machines with no custom start-up files
  • Fixed /rewind sometimes restoring an older version of a file when two queued prompts, or stacked skills, ran together right after a turn that changed it
  • Fixed text and images added when approving a permission prompt being dropped when the approved command or tool then failed
  • Fixed MCP resources from claude.ai connectors and plugin servers not being attached when @-mentioned in the terminal's prompt box
  • Fixed an MCP server that subagents declare being shut down when one of them finished, while other subagents or the session were still using it
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome staying "not connected" after a brief connection problem, even though Chrome was open and signed in
  • Fixed terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock (Mantle) started with no model selected ignoring a pinned Opus model, and still calling an unavailable default model after announcing a fallback
  • Fixed the rest of what you were typing being lost when a plan arrived in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed claude.ai connectors with different names being dropped when they share a server URL (#101856)
  • Fixed plugins going missing from the installed list when several claude plugin commands ran at the same time
  • Fixed task dependencies and metadata being lost when several task updates ran at the same time
  • Fixed incomplete backups of ~/.claude.json being kept, and displacing good ones, when the disk was full
  • Fixed a long pause in Code Mode after code that read hundreds of files in projects with path-scoped rules or Read deny rules
  • Fixed the built-in chart tool failing when Claude called it in Code Mode
  • Fixed Code Mode ignoring an MCP tool's request to end the turn from a script in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Fixed Code Mode in auto mode dropping earlier thinking and rewriting the prompt cache when a mod added a note after a script loaded a skill
  • Fixed Code Mode not restoring a file that a script had read after Esc and /compact
  • Fixed /context undercounting system tools in Code Mode before Claude's first reply
  • Fixed a stopped background subagent sometimes not staying stopped
  • Fixed Claude still waiting for a background agent that was stopped just as it finished, in sessions run by an app or the SDK
  • Fixed background sessions sometimes waking in their previous permission mode after approving a plan
  • Remote Control: Fixed the note about background agents ended by a Stop from a phone or the web showing in the terminal as if you had typed it
  • Remote Control: Fixed the mobile apps hiding the Diff and pull request buttons, or showing a stopped session as working, after turning it on mid-conversation
  • Fixed environment variables written by a SessionStart hook being lost with claude -p --continue
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 with no message when its output went to a file on a full disk: it now prints an error and exits 1, though a full NFS export may go unnoticed
  • Fixed the system prompt keeping the earlier model's instructions when the model was changed after /context but before the first message
  • Fixed Claude sometimes replying to its commit attribution reminder and ending the turn early after the model changed mid-turn; it can still happen where managed settings set the PR attribution line
  • Fixed Esc not ending an LSP tool call that was waiting for a slow or stuck language server
  • Fixed LSP tool calls and diagnostics failing when several calls or edits arrived while a language server was still starting
  • Fixed /mcp listing plugin servers as built-in: they now stand under "Plugin MCPs", --mcp-config and built-in servers under "Other MCPs", and a server's page names its plugin
  • Fixed an "MCP server blocked by enterprise policy: easel" warning showing at every start when an MCP allowlist or denylist excludes the built-in chart tool, which stays blocked
  • Fixed /stats counting new activity in UTC days instead of your local time zone
  • Fixed /ultrareview failing or reviewing the wrong code after the shell moved into another repository: it now stops and names both folders
  • Fixed Grep reporting no matches when the pattern held a line break without multiline mode; it now reports the rejected pattern
  • Fixed Jupyter notebooks saved with a byte order mark being reported as invalid JSON by the Read and NotebookEdit tools
  • Fixed link reference definitions being dropped from CLAUDE.md and memory files that contain an HTML comment
  • Fixed running Monitors keeping the earlier conversation in memory until they end
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending a turn with "Prompt is too long" when a PDF larger than the context window followed a long conversation
  • Fixed the choice between two user or project agent files declaring the same name depending on the order the file search listed them
  • Fixed claude daemon logs never exiting inside a git repository when there is no log file
  • Fixed markdown hiding a character or two after bold or italic text when a backslash came before an emoji later in the paragraph
  • Fixed Edit refusing some valid hook commands in Claude settings files
  • Fixed Read with a page range showing both halves of a scanned two-page spread on each of its pages
  • Fixed line breaks and class stereotypes missing from Mermaid diagrams in HTML artifacts
  • Fixed the Project instructions picker in /config showing only one of its four choices in a 24-row fullscreen window
  • Fixed a subagent's own subagents and forks running on the plan-mode model in plan mode under opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed WebFetch page summaries ignoring the /effort level when a gateway refuses the small fast model
  • Fixed claude -p on Google Cloud's Agent Platform ignoring --settings '{"fastMode":true}' when the model comes from ANTHROPIC_MODEL or a settings file; such runs now bill at the fast mode price
  • Fixed startup under forceLoginOrgUUID being refused after one temporary server error or dropped connection
  • Fixed claude mcp remove giving no way forward for a claude.ai connector: it now says to turn it off in /mcp or remove it on claude.ai
  • Fixed the /mcp "Connect on claude.ai" check saying "not connected" when claude.ai has a connector at the server's URL without its query
  • Fixed /install-github-app and /design-login showing a generic failure for an account on hold instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link
  • Fixed a running MCP task being reported as stopped when you move a session to the background; the background session can now follow the task, but not if its server uses stdio or sets headers
  • Fixed self-hosted runners ignoring a session until they exited, after its failure report was lost or the session was given back to the same runner
  • Fixed self-hosted sessions losing the prompt cache and earlier thinking when the list of repositories a restart couldn't prepare changed
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed tool calls behind a permission prompt vanishing with no result when a new runner took over the prompt, in sessions with telemetry off
  • Fixed resumed self-hosted runner sessions starting without their pushed work in large repositories when --push-outcome-on-release is set
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions being shown as working when Claude Code hangs at every start and --startup-timeout-min is from 2 to about 6
  • Fixed pkill -f in self-hosted runner sessions on Linux ending its own shell with exit code 144, or the runner (needs a pkill with --ignore-ancestors)
  • Fixed scheduled tasks on self-hosted runners having no tool to notify their owner when telemetry is off or a third-party provider is used
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed one slow spawn-runner hook keeping the orchestrator from claiming sessions for its free slots; it now polls every 4 to 6 seconds while a slot is free
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a 403, such as an IP allowlist's, logged as a bad secret or token: most such lines now lead with the server's reason, so update log alerts that match the old words
  • Fixed self-hosted runners' warn mode for repository settings stopping at the first finding of most kinds: it now goes on, up to 50 for a session, and says if it stops early
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed runners that start on a full disk taking sessions and failing them; they now wait for room and exit 1 after a minute with no session, unless started from a work order
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start suggesting a retry when the runner's machine had no git credentials; the error now says whom to ask and what to do if the repository is wrong
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner's last_poll_age_seconds reading 0 while the runner had never polled successfully
  • Fixed the notice about a skipped scheduled task that names no organization: it now says to start Claude Code with --resume, because /resume inside a running session doesn't run the task
  • Fixed claude plugin validate wrongly warning that a mod's AbovePrompt or AbovePromptList hook never runs in VS Code
  • Fixed /design-sync deleting a file it had just uploaded when Claude Design stored that file under a changed name
  • Reverted 2.1.329's removal of the automatic retry when max_tokens exceeds a model's or gateway's limit
  • Improved the claude.ai sign-in link shown by /login, claude auth login and claude setup-token: it is now much shorter
  • Windows: Improved Grep and Glob speed by no longer starting a console host for each built-in ripgrep search on a local path
  • Improved the speed of file diffs
  • Improved /config search: most settings whose name starts with what you type come first, "effort" finds Model, and "dark" or "light" finds Theme
  • Improved /resume: sessions where you only opened a screen such as /model and left are no longer listed
  • Improved Reconnect in /mcp and /plugin: a server's page now stays open, with the cause in view, when the server still fails or needs sign-in
  • Improved the error on macOS when sandbox deny lists are too long: it now names the long lists and how to shorten them
  • Improved /plugin in fullscreen mode: the page of a plugin with errors now starts with those errors
  • Improved /ultrareview's cost confirmation on Team and Enterprise plans: it now says how much of your monthly spend limit is left when that is less than a review usually costs
  • Improved self-hosted runner sessions on Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud's Agent Platform to say so when they start on another default model because your account refused the first
  • Windows: Improved the error when a session's folder is on a drive Claude Code can't verify: it says why, and whether retrying can help
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told how to look at images and PDFs
  • Improved Code Mode: after Esc, "Interrupted" now shows under the stopped command in place of a red error
  • Improved Code Mode: the terminal freezes for far less time after a subagent's script makes thousands of tool calls
  • Changed recurring scheduled tasks and /loop to run up to 30 days instead of 7 while their session keeps running, and say when they end; tasks made before this release still end at 7 days
  • Changed more rm commands aimed at the root, home, a top-level folder or the working folder to ask for approval; where nobody can answer, they're refused
  • Changed deniedMcpServers name entries to hide only the named claude.ai connector, not others at its URL; to block them all, deny its exact URL
  • Changed claude --teleport in some setups to print the git commands for switching branch instead of running them; with -p it exits 1 until you switch
  • Changed unrecognized model names containing "sonnet" or "haiku" to use the shorter system prompt, like other unrecognized names; CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 gives every model the full one
  • Changed skills that Claude runs with a model setting, other than context: fork skills, to leave subagents, forks, compaction and /recap on the session's model
  • Changed a subagent's model fallback to carry over: agents with no model and forks it then starts run on the fallback, and the agents they start use its Bedrock region
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed spawn-runner hooks to start while earlier ones still run, up to --hook-concurrency per orchestrator (4 by default); set it to 1 if yours can't run beside another
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed Bash commands to skip the file diff when nothing needs it, so transcripts can lack it; set bashEditDiffEnabled to true in managed settings to get every diff
  • Changed self-hosted runners to stop a session's start at once, without trying other runners, when a checkout hook exits with status 108
  • Changed prompt hooks to accept model aliases such as haiku or sonnet in their model field
  • Changed /design-sync's fallback build of the reference Storybook to use only a Storybook installed in the project
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions signed in to a Claude apps gateway to be written from short notes instead of the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • [VSCode] Added /fork to fork a conversation after its last reply (#69272)
  • [VSCode] Added /workflows, which opens the agent map with running workflows
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.escapeStopsClaude setting; turn it off so Escape does not stop Claude (#91536)
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.pinPrompt setting to let your message scroll away instead of staying pinned
  • [VSCode] Added the claudeCode.contextUsageThreshold setting for when the context indicator shows (#93036)
  • [VSCode] Added a prompt argument to the "Open in Side Bar" command for keybindings and extensions
  • [VSCode] Added Move up and Move down to a session group's menu (#98654)
  • [VSCode] Fixed VS Code opening and focusing its terminal on every prompt of a connected terminal session
  • [VSCode] Fixed copying a code block adding a trailing newline that ran the command on paste (#96976)
  • [VSCode] Fixed holding Enter on /rewind restoring files, and a double click on Remove or Delete removing a memory, MCP server or plugin marketplace, without confirmation
  • [VSCode] Fixed Enter on a question card sending your earlier answer instead of picking the focused one, and arrow keys not working after an "Other" answer; answered questions reopen on your pick
  • [VSCode] Fixed a held-down Enter key sending a half-written message or running a typed slash command
  • [VSCode] Fixed Cmd+A, C, V, X and Z not working in the rename box and dialogs on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed Ctrl+F and Ctrl+P not moving the caret in the message box on macOS
  • [VSCode] Fixed the Accept and Reject buttons doing nothing on a proposed diff moved to a new window
  • [VSCode] Fixed Accept and Reject Proposed Changes showing over the chat, the terminal tab and other files; they now show only on the proposed diff
  • [VSCode] Fixed a slow-starting Claude tab taking the keyboard away from the file you had gone on typing in
  • [VSCode] Fixed unsaved changes and new problems being missed on macOS and Linux for files whose path contains #, ? or %20, such as a C# folder
  • [VSCode] Fixed whole-line selections counting one line too many in the selection chip, in @-mentions and in what Claude is told, and file links leaving out the last line of a range
  • [VSCode] Fixed a conversation forked in the panel re-running an old, unanswered prompt by itself after a window reload
  • [VSCode] Fixed a forked conversation running the original conversation's /loop schedules a second time
  • [VSCode] Fixed /clear giving no sign that the session still runs without a newly trusted folder's CLAUDE.md and settings
  • [VSCode] Fixed dialogs closing, and losing typed text, when a text selection was dragged past their edge
  • [VSCode] Fixed advisor calls showing as "Unsupported content type" (#73499, #64158, #90471, #73637)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the session list showing no status for the sidebar chat's session (#93898)
  • [VSCode] Fixed the plan preview's Add Comment button vanishing after a fast double click on a word
  • [VSCode] Fixed long lines cut off in the Edit Notebook Cell row, permission rules squeezed in a narrow panel, hard-to-see question card marks, and menus moving the chat after a declined trust prompt
  • [VSCode] Fixed signing in to an account on hold showing a generic failure instead of the on-hold notice and appeal link

items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Highlights

Extensible KV cache, on by default

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

  • Model Runner V1 removed (#63373).
    • VLLM_USE_V2_MODEL_RUNNER and VllmConfig.use_v2_model_runner are gone; setting the env var to anything but 1 fails at startup.

    • Deprecated: parallel_drafting, capture_torch_profiler, enable_layerwise_nvtx_tracing.
  • Default --block-size is 64 instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit --block-size still wins.
  • gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704).
  • ROCm 7.2 wheels and -rocm72 images are no longer published (#61939).
  • Removed:
    • QuTLASS and the fp_quant method (#65230).
    • Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE; use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG (#65542).

  • Model and plugin code: all process_weights_after_loading hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config compute_hash() replaced by compile_factors() / hash_config() (#65652).
  • API behavior:
    • llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569).
    • Canary transcription without language returns 400 (#65445).
    • An empty tools array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854).
    • /v1/systemone rejects request-supplied chat templates without --trust-request-chat-template (#64503).

  • New defaults:
